items.title: Jensen Huang is reinstated as Nvidia CEO
items.content_html:
Despite multiple controversies and Nvidia's board announcing it would not reinstate Jensen Huang, the firm's co-founder is right back as CEO.

Following the direct intervention of President Trump, Huang is reinstated with immediate affect, after what CNBC reports were a series of discussions between him and Nvidia's board. Nvidia stock immediately climbed by over 30% as of 9:30 AM ET.

The White House has issued a statement praising the reinstatement. "President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the Nvidia board," it said. "We have to protect our geniuses."

Alongside this, the Nvidia board has said that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government," and that it is confident Huang "poses no national security risk."

Chair of the board, Harvey C. Jones, had been the one to address Huang's departure during Nvidia's latest earnings call. He was very firm that Huang would not be returning, but he makes no mention of that position now.

Instead, Jones has issued a statement welcoming back Huang.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," he said. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."

Interim CEO Colette Kress has reportedly clashed in the past clashed with Huang over his circular economy. This is the policy where Nvidia pays firms to buy from it, on the presumption that the expected massive profits from AI will eventually pay off.

Huang has publicly thanked Kress as she resumes her Chief Financial Officer duties, and praised Jones for his leadership as chair.

"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," said Huang in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."

"I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process," he continued.

National security

Perhaps key to Huang being allowed to return as CEO is how Nvidia has revised its national security procedures. On November 17, 2026, five days after Huang resigned, Nvidia announced the creation of an Export Control Oversight Committee.

"As the world's leading advanced computing company, NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges [of national security]," said Harvey Jones.


Trump (shown here during his first administration) told Nvidia that Huang has done nothing wrong — image credit: White House

There was no comment on what procedures Nvidia had followed before, nor any acknowledgement that the new committee followed the controversy over Huang.

Instead, Jones said that the decision "to create this new committee reflects the Board's further commitment to enhance its engagement with relevant government stakeholders, and to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight."

Huang's resignation

The news comes after Huang said that he would return to Nvidia if the company would just ask him. The company then said it would not.

Huang resigned as CEO. The board unanimously accepted that resignation, after his multiple affairs were revealed to include one with an alleged Chinese spy.

He was replaced by Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. People including Elon Musk and President Trump, however, called for his reinstatement.

How we got here

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, and the company initially became known for producing gaming processors. However, demand for AI processors starting in late 2022 saw Nvidia's stock rise 14-fold.

The latest available figures showed that this earned Huang a personal net worth of $90 billion by May 2024. However, Nvidia's stock dropped by over $800 billion after the first revelations of Huang's affairs emerged.


Jensen Huang (left) was briefly replaced by Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress (right) as interim CEO. - images credit: Nvidia.

Ultimately he would be shown to have had three affairs, but it was the one with Alice Huang (no familial relation) that prompted the controversy. Alice Huang is alleged to have been a Chinese spy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce launched a joint investigation into the issues.

Those issues are partly that Jensen Huang may have been targeted in a Chinese intelligence operation, and therefore he may have provided confidential information. There is also a question of whether Nvidia, under Huang's leadership, has violated US export controls.

Megaspeed, a Singapore firm which had Alice Huang as an executive until August 2025, is being investigated over allegations that it provided restricted processors to China.

Alongside both of these, there is a question of how much Huang and other executives knew. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said on November 19, 2026, that the DOJ was looking into whether "Nvidia misled investors and the public" about the risk of China obtaining restricted processors.

As yet there has been no word on whether Huang's reinstatement affects this DOJ investigation. At present, however, a Congressional hearing is to be held in public and live-streamed on December 3, 2026.

Chair Harvey Jones has said that Nvidia's own investigation is to continue.

items.title: Apple sued for $162M in India over NameDrop patent infringement
items.content_html:
Apple has been sued by a startup in India, demanding $161.9 million and an iPhone sales injunction over alleged patent infringement by contact-sharing feature NameDrop.

Apple introduced NameDrop in iOS 17 as a way for users to quickly share contact details with each other by bringing iPhones close together. Three years after it became available to use by the public, Apple's now being sued over the feature.

The lawsuit in India by GG Technologies accuses Apple of infringing on an Indian patent, reports TechCrunch. The patent covers ways for phones to exchange contact details with others nearby, without requiring a manual pairing process beforehand.

This was implemented in a GG Technologies app, StayTouch, which is available for iOS and Android. The app was launched in 2019, and filed for patent protection in the U.S. the same year.

An Indian patent application was filed in 2021, and was awarded in July 2024. Meanwhile, Apple introduced NameDrop during WWDC 2023.

The lawsuit seeks 15 billion rupees ($161.86 million) in damages from Apple. It also wants an injunction to limit the NameDrop feature itself, demanding restrictions of the sale of iPhones and Apple Watches in India with NameDrop preloaded.

The 781-page filing at the Bombay High Court hasn't been granted a hearing date at this time, but one is expected soon.

Expensive contacts

The lawsuit is not the first time Apple has heard of the complaint. Indeed, the companies have already argued over the matter for months.

GG Technologies said it had filed the lawsuit in India in October, but only after mediation proceedings failed. Mediation started in April and ended in September.

In India, it is usually required for companies to attempt to mediate the matter before a commercial lawsuit is filed with the court.

It's also not the only lawsuit Apple faces. At the same time as starting mediation, GG Technologies sued Apple for patent infringement in April.

In August 2026, the US International Trade Commission opened its own patent infringement investigation.

items.title: Sunday Reboot: Siri AI limits and the possibility of pettiness
items.content_html:
In this week's Sunday Reboot, Apple's pettiness is on full display in the UK, though it's entirely unclear why Apple decided not to extend Siri AI limit increases to the country.

Sunday Reboot is a weekly column covering some of the lighter stories within the Apple reality distortion field from the past seven days. All to get next week underway with a good first step.

Higher limits, but not for these specific countries

As an organization, Apple has disagreements with practically every major government on the planet in some form. Most of the time, it's business as usual and doesn't affect the normal services Apple provides to customers.

Most, that is, not all of the time. Sometimes, Apple makes decisions against specific entities benefiting from something that everyone else already enjoys.

A big example of that is the whole EU Digital Markets Act spat, which basically enabled Apple to stop some AI-based services from working in the bloc at all. All under the claim that there needs to be a way to preserve privacy despite the EU's regulation.

That's been a problem that has persisted for many years, and will still do for years to come. Sadly, it's a glacial experience waiting for a multinational giant and a continental government agency to blink first.

At the very least, there's some rhyme or reason for that happening at all.

Siri AI limit increases are happening for iCloud+ subscribers, except not in the UK for some reason... - Image Credit: Parliament

When it comes to Apple's decision to introduce daily Siri AI allowances, Apple wasn't so forthcoming with a reason.

On November 16, Apple said that there were allowance extensions for subscribers of iCloud+. It was available everywhere Siri AI was potentially usable, except a small list of regions.

China makes sense to be excluded, as it doesn't have Siri AI yet. So do EU countries in general, as it's a continuation of the existing spat.

However, for Brazil, South Korea, and the United Kingdom, there's no immediately apparent reason at all from Apple.

For the UK, it's especially annoying, since we have Siri AI access enabled already. All the block does is stop iCloud+ subscribers from being able to get more allowance.

It is an extraordinarily picky decision to prevent the UK from getting more of a benefit from something it already can use. Blocking access completely to something when it wasn't available before would make more sense, but this doesn't.

Maybe it's justifiable?

Sure, Apple and the UK don't see eye to eye on matters like the App Store and continual demands for backdoor access to iCloud data. Heck, Apple even turned off Advanced Data Protection in the UK in early 2025 because of a law change, and refused to reinstate it.

It doesn't help the UK that a tribunal ruled in favor of Apple on November 19, forcing the UK government to admit there was an order to try and get access to encrypted user data.

To be clear here, the problem is less about the existence of the demand for access, as that's something everyone's complained about previously in various ways. The issue is the UK deciding to use laws to try and gag Apple from discussing the matter at all.

The UK government gag order certainly prevented Apple from talking, and to its credit, it stayed quiet. It's just that the UK government didn't take into account that media in other countries would report about it.

It's one thing for Apple to be ordered to do something and to resist every step of the way. It's another to keep an order that affects the general public hidden from view.

Apple blocked ADP in the UK over encryption-breaking demands and regulation. The Siri AI thing seems trivial in comparison.

We don't know if Apple is lashing out at the UK with this Siri AI limit exclusion because of this matter. The timing is very coincidental, but it also seems like an extremely unusually minor response compared to closing access to an entire service, as it did before.

As it stands, the decision to not allow more of a Siri AI limit to people paying for iCloud+ in the UK is a very picky and petty thing to do, seemingly without that much tech-wise to get in the way.

It's the country-wide version of Apple wishing you to have an annoying, ever-present bubble under your iPhone's screen protector.

It's mildly annoying, but more confusing about why the decision was made in the first place.

Hopefully Apple will eventually give some explanation, even a half-hearted one, to nod for why this has happened.

As it stands, all we can do is make wild speculation and imagine Apple with a chip on its shoulder. One that only it knows why it exists.

Last week's Sunday Reboot discussed the commentator's curse with CEO antics, and whether hardware reviewers need to learn new skills like robotics.

items.title: Google's AI search monetization failure is costing Apple revenue
items.content_html:
Apple's Safari search deal with Google isn't quite as lucrative as it once was, with changes in the way people search seemingly to blame.

Apple and Google have a well-established agreement that has earned itself legal trouble, such as an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice. However, while the $20 billion deal for Google to be the preferred search engine of Safari, the relationship is starting to falter.

Not because of a problem between Google and Apple, but more because users are changing the way they search to rely more on AI. That, and Google's struggling to monetize the change.

Evidence of this, according to The Information, was in the quarterly financial results, with Apple's Services arm slowing growth from 12% to 10% year-over-year. Apple executives also said that a further cooling is to be expected for the next quarter.

Google, meanwhile, saw its shares drop 18% since it reported a downturn in search advertising revenue growth. This was down to the increased popularity of things like AI search results.

According to Rosenblatt Securities senior research analyst Barton Crockett, Google wasn't able to monetize AI overviews to the same level as normal search results. That's apparently surfacing in Apple's deceleration of Services.

Google's ad monetization for searches in AI mode was lower than for traditional searches, despite continued year-on-year growth in queries. Search ad revenue growth slowed to 12%, down from 17% in the previous quarter.

An Apple revenue hit

The rise in AI usage and the lower monetization of AI searches is something that also affects Apple. That search deal between the two companies has Google paying Apple 36% of the revenue generated from search ads seen through Safari.

If there's a reduction in search ad revenue, that's going to also hit what Google ultimately pays Apple under the deal.

As for what Google can do to fix things, it is still working on experimenting with its AI features. However, it is cautious about scaring users away by including too many ads or changing formats.

There's also how users search with AI using longer and broader queries versus traditional search. Apparently, that style of query is harder to monetize.

Advertisers do hope that Google will be able to work out how to show those AI search ads to regain revenue more effectively. It could lead to a revenue rebound, and for Apple to earn more from the agreement once again.

items.title: Bumper crop of spring launches go way beyond just iPhone 18
items.content_html:
Apple's spring launch lineup is expected to be very busy, with an OLED iPad Air, iPhone Air 2, the non-Pro iPhone 18 lineup among others.

The fall release season was busy, but that doesn't mean there will be fewer items for Apple to launch in the spring. It seems that Apple has more items than ever to bring out early in 2027.

In Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman writes that the 27.4 system software cycle will arrive between February and March. For the most part, the products are largely known about or are at least already expected to arrive during that time.

Apple is expected to launch the standard iPhone 18 at the same time. Apple has changed the cadence of its iPhone launches, delaying the standard non-Pro models so there are two launches per year.

The iPhone 18 will also be joined by the iPhone Air 2. Also expected in the spring is an OLED iPad Air, which should launch with the improved display technology in both sizes using the tech.

The refresh of the iPad Pro line should also take place at the same time, moving the models to the M6 chip. There will also be a similar spec-bump update to the MacBook Air, as well as to the MacBook Neo.

More, more, more

While Gurman points out that the launches will be centered around the usual March launch period that Apple has used before, it won't necessarily be the case for everything.

Indeed, the listed products are items expected in the first half of 2027 in general. It just so happens that it lines up with the usual March event timing.

Under the management of new CEO John Ternus, it may not be kept as one event. Based on claims Ternus wants more frequent releases, this could mean more launch events throughout the period instead of just one.

As for the rest of the year, Gurman adds that there are many products inbound later in the year to still get excited about, without going into detail.

His broad list includes the usual expectation of the iPhone 20, which should land in the fall, as well as an update to the Apple Watch line.

He also adds that there's the smart glasses project that's still due to arrive in 2027. Along with it, the fabled AirPods with cameras.

items.title: New MacBook Neo now expected in spring 2027
items.content_html:
It's always been clear that a MacBook Neo refresh is coming. A new report slightly refines the timetable for the new model, and new colors may arrive with that update too.

Among the multiple previous reports of Apple planning a second-generation MacBook Neo, Bloomberg said that one would be released in the first half of 2027. Now the same publication is back to narrow that down further to spring.

Specifically, the new claim is that this second MacBook New is codenamed J701, and that Apple will release subsequent generations annually. It's said that it is to match the release cycle of the MacBook Pro and the MacBook Air, and that Apple is aiming it at the Chromebook and lower-cost Windows PC market.

The report also speculates that the major update will be replacing the current model's A18 Pro processor with an A19 Pro. It cautiously reports that there may be frequent refreshes of the MacBook Neo that only mean it getting different colors.

So the report's only new elements that perhaps came from sources rather than predictions, are the annual update cycle and the spring launch. That there is to be an update is unsurprising, given the enormous success of the original model.

The guess that new versions will target Chromebook and Windows PC buyers can't even be called surprising, since it is precisely what the original MacBook Neo has done. In November 2026, Apple sold 170,000 of the MacBook Neo to education in the Philippines, for instance.

Then the MacBook Neo's existence was in part because Apple had binned versions of the A18 Pro processor that would otherwise be wasted. So the speculation of a move to the A19 Pro as used in the iPhone 17 range, is practically inevitable.

What hasn't been predicted much before is this idea that Apple may produce the next MacBook Neo in different colors. Previously it has often updated the colors on the consumer iMac, although not with the latest release.

items.title: Black Friday OLED TV deals start at $699, with up to $1,400 off LG, Sony & Samsung

Black Friday OLED TV deals have dropped LG's 55-inch B6E to $699.99 at Best Buy, with savings reaching up to $1,400 off larger, premium models from LG, Sony, and Samsung.

OLED televisions use self-lit pixels to deliver deep blacks, rich colors, and precise contrast without the backlighting found in conventional LED TVs. Their higher prices have traditionally been a barrier, but the latest discounts put several 2026 models within reach of shoppers looking to upgrade.

Get OLED Black Friday deals

Best Buy has discounted LG's B6E, C6, and G6 lineups, along with competing models from Sony and Samsung. Amazon is also matching Best Buy's $1,399.99 price on the 65-inch LG C6.

Black Friday OLED TV deals start at $699.99

Here are six OLED TV deals worth considering:

  • LG 55-inch B6E OLED - $699.99 ($700 off) at Best Buy
  • LG 65-inch B6E OLED - $999.99 ($900 off) at Best Buy
  • Sony 65-inch BRAVIA 6 OLED - $1,199.99 ($800 off) at Best Buy
  • LG 65-inch C6 OLED - $1,399.99 ($1,300 off) at Amazon and Best Buy
  • Samsung 65-inch S90H OLED - $1,399.99 ($1,300 off) at Amazon and Best Buy
  • LG 65-inch G6 OLED - $1,999.99 ($1,400 off) at Best Buy

LG's B6E offers the least expensive way into the lineup, with Dolby Vision, a 120Hz refresh rate, and support for NVIDIA G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium. Its Alpha 8 AI Processor Gen3 handles picture processing, while LG's webOS platform provides access to streaming apps.

The 65-inch B6E is particularly appealing at $999.99, giving buyers 10 more inches of screen size (measured diagonally) for $300 more. Both sizes share the same core features, making the decision largely a matter of budget and available space.

For another $200, Sony's 65-inch BRAVIA 6 brings the company's picture processing and Google TV platform into the mix. It supports Dolby Vision and 4K gaming at 120Hz, making it another option for movies, streaming, and console gaming.

LG's C6 and Samsung's S90H compete directly at $1,399.99, although they take different approaches. The C6 uses Brightness Booster technology and LG's Alpha 11 AI Processor Gen3, while Samsung emphasizes its Glare Free screen treatment to reduce distracting reflections.

Both support refresh rates up to 165Hz with compatible gaming PCs, giving them an advantage over the 120Hz models for high-refresh-rate gaming. However, LG supports Dolby Vision, while Samsung uses HDR10+ instead.

LG OLED AI television

At the top of the list, LG's 65-inch G6 costs $1,999.99 after a $1,400 discount. Its higher brightness, Reflection Free Premium technology, and gallery-style design make it appealing for wall-mounted installations, although buyers should know that the included flush wall mount doesn't come with a tabletop stand.

All six televisions can connect to an Apple TV 4K through HDMI, and AirPlay support lets iPhone, iPad, and Mac users stream compatible content directly to the televisions. Apple TV 4K owners who want Dolby Vision should consider the LG or Sony models, since Samsung doesn't support the format.

For most shoppers, the 65-inch LG B6E at $999.99 offers the strongest combination of screen size, features, and price. The C6 and S90H provide worthwhile upgrades for buyers who prioritize gaming or reflection handling, while the G6 caters to those willing to pay more for premium picture performance and design.

Hallmark+ stands out for holiday viewing, with three months of discounted streaming instead of the two offered by most participating channels. Its catalog includes Christmas movies and original programming, making the promotion particularly well-timed.

BritBox and PBS Masterpiece offer inexpensive ways to catch up on British dramas and mysteries, while MGM+ and AMC+ provide additional movies and original series.

Prime Video Black Friday deals start at $1.75 per month

Amazon also carries discounted subscriptions to Apple TV, Paramount+, and Crunchyroll, so existing Prime Video customers can get many of the same deals without signing up directly through each service.

A Prime membership or standalone Prime Video subscription is required to purchase these add-on channels. The discounted prices don't include the cost of that underlying subscription.

Black Friday streaming deals won't last forever

Most of these Black Friday streaming discounts are scheduled to end November 30, which is Cyber Monday. However, the length of the promotional subscription matters just as much as the advertised price.

Apple TV and Crunchyroll offer six months of savings, while Paramount+ and most Prime Video channels provide only two discounted months. Starz offers the strongest long-term bargain for customers willing to pay $11.99 upfront for a year.

The promotions generally renew automatically at their regular prices when the discounted periods end, and eligibility varies between services.

Anyone planning to subscribe should check the renewal price before completing checkout. These Black Friday deals can make streaming considerably cheaper, but keeping several subscriptions after their promotions expire can quickly erase those savings.

items.title: Apple supplier TSMC cuts off China chip orders amid tighter export controls
items.content_html:
TSMC, a key Apple supplier and the company that makes its A- and M-series iPhone and Mac chips, has suspended some advanced chip orders for Chinese companies following the tightening of United States semiconductor export restrictions.

Under the revised rules, TSMC can no longer provide Chinese companies with chips built using the 16nm or smaller manufacturing process. That is, unless a U.S. export license has been granted or they qualify for an exemption.

This new restriction means that Chinese companies are limited to chips that use much older technology built on the 28nm or 40nm processes. As a result, they will not be able to make use of the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) employed by AI data centers.

That may be key to the tightening restrictions. U.S. company Nvidia, which is going through its own struggles, is at the forefront of the AI chip market. By limiting Chinese companies to older chip technology, the U.S. could hope to protect Nvidia from growing competition.

A change in process

Impact Newswire reports that, prior to this recent change, TSMC was able to assess a customer's chip designs and then determine whether they qualified for an exemption to U.S. export requirements. But that's now changed, with Chinese companies needing to get a license or exemption ahead of time.

That has left TSMC in a difficult position, and it's told customers that they must suspend orders of 16nm chips or smaller. The orders will resume if customers secure U.S. approval.

While the U.S. does maintain a list of approved companies, none of them are Chinese companies. The list includes the likes of Apple, AMD, and Nvidia.

TSMC has said that it intends to comply with the new law changes around export controls to Chinese companies. That's unsurprising given the possible fallout if it chose not to.

TSMC relies heavily on custom from U.S. companies like Apple, and not complying with export rules could put that business in jeopardy. Aside from the potential fines associated with non-compliance, U.S. companies could be barred from doing business with TSMC entirely.

The company also uses U.S. electronic design automation (EDA) software to manufacture its most advanced chips. Losing access to that software could be catastrophic for TSMC's business.

items.title: First iPhone Air 2 & iPhone 18 dummy units don't have any surprises
items.content_html:
With Apple expected to announce the iPhone Air 2 and iPhone 18 in early 2027, the first dummy units have been photographed and appear to confirm that the iPhone Air's biggest problem will finally be addressed.

September 2026 saw Apple change the way it announces iPhones, with just the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo unveiled. But early 2027 is set to see Apple announce yet more models as it switches to a twice-yearly release cadence.

As part of that, the iPhone Air 2 and iPhone 18 are expected to be joined by the iPhone 18e in the spring of 2027. Now, two of those devices appear to have debuted in dummy unit form.

Shared by serial leaker Sonny Dickson via his X social media account, two images show the front and back of the devices. There are few surprises for those who have been following along with recent rumors, but confirmation of what we can expect is always welcome.

The big changes

The most notable change that iPhone Air 2 buyers can look forward to is the addition of a second camera. The current iPhone Air has a single 48-megapixel camera, and that's something that has long been a knock against that device for some.

With iPhone Air 2, Apple is expected to add a second camera in the form of an ultra wide option. There won't be any optical zoom here, though, so you'll still need an iPhone 18 Pro model for that.

One change that isn't shown in the dummy unit for obvious reasons is the chip. The iPhone Air 2 is set to use the A20 Pro, bringing improved performance and battery life.

We've also been told to expect the iPhone Air 2 to be even thinner than its predecessor, too. But Dickson didn't share measurements, and it's hard to tell from the photos.

As for the base-model iPhone 18, that's set to use the A20 chip and be the cut-down Pro model that we're accustomed to. We don't expect there to be any major design changes compared with the previous-gen iPhone 17, although new colors are likely.
